transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you or what brings you in today?

Hi. Thanks for seeing me. Um, so I came in because I keep getting these... these really nagging thoughts that I’ve missed some tiny mistake in a layout, or that I accidentally sent the wrong version of a file to a client. 

Actually, just last Tuesday I was working with this new client—they own that little artisan soap shop downtown? The one that smells overwhelmingly like lavender when you walk past? I love their products, but their branding was just a nightmare to overhaul because they wanted everything to look "rustic but modern," which is completely an oxymoron if you ask me. I spent hours just trying to find the perfect typeface that didn't look like a generic wedding invitation. 

But anyway, um, sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right. Even when I can look at the screen and see that the layout is probably fine, my mind just keeps circling back to it. Like, I just can't let the thought go.
When you have these thoughts about making a mistake, how do they make you feel emotionally? Do they cause you significant distress or anxiety?

Um, yeah, they do make me anxious. It's like this buzzing feeling in my chest that just won't quit until I check the file again. It's really frustrating, especially when I'm trying to relax at home. 

Actually, speaking of relaxing, I tried to take a bath the other night with one of those soaps from the new client—the lavender one I mentioned? I thought it would help me unwind, but the whole time I was just staring at the bathroom tiles. Did you know the grout in my bathroom is this awful off-white color? It drives me crazy. I've been meaning to regrout it for months, but every time I go to the hardware store, I get overwhelmed by all the different shades of white. There's, like, "eggshell" and "alabaster" and "navajo white," and it's just... who needs that many whites? 

But, um, anyway, yeah, the thoughts definitely make me feel pretty anxious. It's not, like, completely ruining my life or anything, but it's definitely a nuisance.
When these anxious thoughts come up, do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking things over and over, organizing, or trying to neutralize the thought in some way?

Um, yeah, I do. Before I submit any work now, I have this whole routine. I'll re-open the file, compare all the layers, re-save it, and then I kind of... mentally walk through every single design choice one more time. It's like I have to justify it to myself. 

Which reminds me, I actually had to explain my design choices to my sister last weekend. She’s redoing her kitchen—finally getting rid of those horrible 90s oak cabinets. I told her she should go with a sage green, but she is dead set on navy blue. Navy blue! In a kitchen that gets almost no natural light! I tried to explain color theory to her, how dark colors absorb light and make a small space feel even more cramped, but she just showed me this Pinterest board full of these massive, brightly lit farmhouse kitchens and said, "But it looks so cozy!" I mean, it's her house, but I just know she's going to regret it by Christmas. 

Oh, right, sorry. Um, but yeah, doing all that checking with the files... it doesn't take over my whole day or anything, but it definitely makes me slower. I just feel a lot less free creatively because I'm so bogged down in making sure every tiny thing is perfectly correct before I can let it go.
Do you feel like you have to do certain things in a very specific way, or else something bad might happen, or you’ll feel even more anxious?

Um, I don't really think so? Like, I don't have a specific thought that something terrible is going to happen if I don't check my files. It's more just... I have to make sure it's right, you know? Otherwise, I just feel off. 

Speaking of feeling off, I had the weirdest interaction at the coffee shop this morning. I usually go to this little place on 4th Street—they roast their own beans, and the barista, I think his name is Leo, always remembers my order. But today, there was a new girl working, and she completely botched it. I asked for an oat milk flat white, and she gave me what I'm pretty sure was a vanilla latte with whole milk. I took one sip and almost gagged. I mean, I'm not lactose intolerant or anything, but whole milk just coats your mouth in this weird way, doesn't it? And vanilla syrup is just so aggressively sweet. I didn't want to be *that* person who complains, so I just smiled and took it, but I ended up throwing it away two blocks down. Five dollars down the drain. 

But, um, anyway... what were you asking? Oh, right, doing things in a specific way. Yeah, I don't think I have a fear of something bad happening. I just don't like the feeling of not being sure if I made a mistake.
When you feel that anxiety about possibly making a mistake, does it feel like you *have* to go back and check or redo things, even if you know it might be unnecessary?

Um, yeah, I guess I do feel like I *have* to do it. Like I was saying before, it's this whole routine before I submit anything now. I'll re-open the file, compare all the layers, re-save it... and then I have to mentally walk through every single design choice one more time. Even if I know I already checked it, I just can't hit send until I do the whole process. 

It's actually kind of like how my neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, handles her recycling. Have you ever noticed how some people are just overly intense about recycling? She will literally wash out every single peanut butter jar until there isn't a speck left, and then she sorts her plastics by number. Which, I mean, is great for the environment, but the other day she came over and knocked on my door because she saw me put a slightly greasy pizza box in my bin. She gave me this whole lecture about how one greasy box can contaminate the entire batch at the facility. And I was just standing there in my pajamas, holding my coffee, thinking, "It's just cardboard, Mrs. Higgins." But she just *has* to make sure everyone on the block is doing it perfectly. 

But, um, anyway... yeah, with my files, I do feel like I have to go back and check. It doesn't, like, consume my entire day, but it definitely slows me down. I just feel so much less free creatively because I'm stuck doing all this checking instead of just designing.
Do you ever have thoughts that come into your mind that feel intrusive or unwanted, and that cause you a lot of anxiety or discomfort?

Yeah, actually, that’s... that’s kind of the main reason I decided to come in. I keep getting these nagging thoughts that I’ve missed some tiny mistake in a layout, or like I’ve accidentally sent the wrong version of a file to a client. 

Which, speaking of clients, I have this one right now for a boutique hotel downtown, and they are an absolute nightmare to work with. They hired me to redesign all their restaurant menus, but they keep changing their minds about the typography every two days. First they wanted Garamond, then they wanted something "more edgy" so we switched to a custom sans-serif, and yesterday—I kid you not—they asked to see a mockup in Papyrus. Papyrus! It’s literally a running joke in the design world. I tried to politely explain that it looks like a cheap yoga studio flyer from 2004, but the owner's wife absolutely loves it. She says it feels "earthy and organic." I swear, I almost fired them on the spot. I just don't understand why people hire a professional if they're just going to insist on the worst possible choices.

But, um... sorry, I got distracted. What were we talking about? Oh, the unwanted thoughts. Right. So, yeah, I'll get this thought that I sent the wrong version or messed up a layout, and even when I can look right at the screen and see it’s probably fine, my mind just keeps circling back to it. It just won't let it go.
When you have these intrusive thoughts about mistakes, do you feel driven to do something—like checking, re-reading, or redoing things—to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah, exactly. It’s like I was mentioning a few minutes ago. When those nagging thoughts pop up, I absolutely feel driven to do my whole routine to make the feeling go away. I’ll go back, re-open the file, compare the layers again, and re-save it. And then I do that mental walkthrough of all my design choices. 

Actually, speaking of saving files, my Mac has been acting so strange lately since I updated the OS. Apple always pushes these updates right when you're in the middle of a massive project, you know? I hit 'remind me tomorrow' for like three weeks, but it finally forced the update on me overnight. And now, every time I use my shortcut keys in Illustrator, there's this tiny half-second lag. It drives me absolutely insane. I even called this freelance IT guy I use, and he told me to reset my wifi router. Like, what does my router have to do with my design software lagging? I swear, sometimes tech support is just reading off a script and they don't even listen to what you're actually saying. 

But, um... sorry. To answer your question, yes. I feel driven to do all that checking and re-saving. Like I said, it doesn’t take over my entire day or anything, but it definitely makes me slower. I just feel so much less free creatively when I have to keep doing it.

Do you ever try to neutralize or get rid of the anxious thoughts by doing something else in your mind, like thinking a specific phrase, counting, or trying to replace the thought with a different one?

Um, like a specific phrase or counting? No, not really. I mean, the main thing I do in my head is what I was talking about earlier—that mental walkthrough. Where I have to mentally retrace every single design choice one more time before I can finally submit the work. I just kind of sit there and review it all in my mind. 

Which is honestly so exhausting, especially when I'm working from coffee shops. Have you noticed how loud they've gotten lately? I used to love going to this little indie place down the street, but they just got a new espresso machine that sounds like an airplane taking off every time they steam milk. And the baristas always have the indie pop music cranked up so high. I tried wearing noise-canceling headphones, but then I get paranoid that someone is trying to talk to me or that I'm breathing too loudly. My friend Sarah told me I should just work from the library, but you can't even have a lidless cup in there, and I absolutely need my iced matcha if I'm going to get through an afternoon of client revisions. 

But anyway, sorry... no, I don't really count or repeat phrases. I just do the whole routine—re-opening the file, comparing the layers, re-saving it, and then doing that mental review of all my choices. It just makes me so much slower, you know? Like I'm just not as free creatively as I used to be.

When you feel anxious about possibly making a mistake in your work, do you feel like you have to do your checking routine to prevent something bad from happening, or to make sure that everything is just right?

I guess it's mostly just needing to make sure everything is exactly right, so I don't send out a mistake. Like I was saying, before I submit work now, I just feel like I have to re-open the file, compare the layers, re-save it, and sometimes mentally walk through every design choice one more time. 

Which, honestly, comparing layers can be such a nightmare anyway if you're collaborating with someone else. Have you ever seen a Photoshop file where a person just leaves everything as 'Layer 1', 'Layer 2', 'Layer 2 copy 3'? It is absolutely infuriating. I took over a project from a junior designer last week, and I swear I spent three hours just grouping and naming his layers before I could even look at the actual layout. I mean, they teach you basic file hygiene in design school, but apparently, nobody pays attention anymore. I always color-code my folders—blue for background assets, red for typography, green for vector smart objects. It just makes life so much easier when you actually respect the workspace, you know? My old creative director used to dock our pay if we handed off a messy file, which sounds harsh, but it really instilled good habits.

But, um... sorry, I'm rambling about work again. What was I saying? Oh, right. Doing the whole checking routine. Yeah, it’s mostly just to make sure it’s all right before it goes out to the client. Like I said, it doesn’t take over my whole day or anything, but it definitely makes me slower. And it just makes me feel so much less free creatively when I have to keep stopping to do it.
Do you ever feel like you have to do certain things a certain number of times, or in a certain way, to make the anxiety go away or to feel like things are balanced or just right?

Um, not really a specific number of times, like counting to five or anything like that. It’s more just... it has to be done in that specific sequence I keep bringing up. I know I sound like a broken record today, but it really is just that before I submit any work now, I have to do it in that exact order—re-open the file, compare the layers, re-save it, and then do that mental walkthrough of all my design choices. 

Actually, speaking of doing things in a specific order, I just started trying to meal prep on Sundays because my sister swore it would save me time during the workweek. But it is honestly such a massive hassle. I even bought all these matching glass containers—because obviously, I can't stand the cheap plastic ones that stain the second you put pasta sauce in them. Have you ever tried to get tomato stains out of Tupperware? It's completely impossible. My mom used to leave them out on the patio in the sun to bleach them, which sounds like some weird old wives' tale, but she absolutely swore by it. Anyway, I spent like four hours last Sunday roasting vegetables and making quinoa, and by Wednesday, I was so sick of looking at it that I just ended up ordering Pad Thai on DoorDash anyway. 

But, um... sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. What were you asking? Oh, doing things a certain way. Yeah, it's really just that same file-checking routine I mentioned. It has to be done that way before I can send the email. Like I said, it doesn’t take over my entire day, but it definitely just makes me so much slower. I just feel a lot less free creatively than I used to.
When you do your checking routine, do you feel that not doing it would lead to a mistake that you couldn’t forgive yourself for, or that something bad would actually happen as a result?

I mean, I don't think someone is going to die or anything if I don't do it. But it's definitely this overwhelming feeling that if I don't do my whole routine—you know, re-opening the file, comparing the layers, re-saving it, and doing that mental walkthrough of my design choices—I'll just make a mistake that I'll look incredibly stupid for. Like, what if I send it to the client and there's a glaring error? 

Which, speaking of clients, I have this one client right now who is just impossible to please. She runs this boutique skincare line, and she wants everything to look "minimalist but warm," which is basically an oxymoron in design. I sent her three different mockups last week, and she rejected all of them because the beige wasn't "inviting" enough. How is beige supposed to be inviting? It's beige! I even tried pulling color palettes from 1970s interior design books because that whole retro aesthetic is really coming back. Have you noticed that? Everyone wants mustard yellow and burnt orange in their living rooms now. My aunt had a burnt orange shag carpet in her house when I was growing up, and I remember thinking it was the ugliest thing in the world. Now people are paying thousands of dollars for vintage rugs that look exactly like it. 

But anyway, sorry, I get so worked up about that client. Um, yeah, if I don't do the checking, I just feel like I'll make a mistake I can't take back. It doesn't consume my entire day, but it definitely slows me down. I just feel so much less free creatively when I have to keep doing it before I submit anything.
Have these thoughts and the need to check your work started to interfere with your daily life, like taking up a lot of time or affecting your ability to do things you normally enjoy?

Well, I mean, I’m still getting my work done, mostly. But I’ve definitely started missing some internal deadlines because of all the extra time it takes. Which is really stressing me out because I’m trying to move toward a creative director role. Our current creative director, Marcus, is actually retiring next year. He’s been at the agency since, like, 1998. He literally still uses a physical Rolodex on his desk. Have you ever actually seen one of those in real life? It is wild. He just sits there spinning this little wheel of paper cards to find our printing vendor's phone number instead of just searching his email. I tried to set him up with a digital contacts list last year, and he looked at me like I had two heads. It’s so funny how people get completely stuck in their ways. My dad is the exact same way, he absolutely refuses to use Google Maps and still prints out MapQuest directions if he goes anywhere new. I don't even know how MapQuest still exists, to be honest, but he finds a way. 

But, um... gosh, I'm sorry, I went totally off track again. You were asking about it interfering with my life. Yeah, so, like I said, I'm missing those internal deadlines. And I’ve also noticed I’m holding back on bolder design ideas lately. I just end up playing it really safe because I’m so afraid I’ll overlook something in a more complex layout and completely damage my chances of getting Marcus's job when he leaves.
When you do your checking routine, does it feel like something bad will happen if you don’t do it, or is it more about reducing the anxiety of possibly making a mistake?

I know I keep saying this, but it really is just about the anxiety of making a mistake. It's not like I think the building is going to burn down. It's just... I have to do that same thing before I submit any work. I re-open the file, I compare all the layers, I re-save it, and then I do that whole mental walkthrough of every single design choice I made. 

Speaking of design choices, I actually just started redecorating my home office because I'm working remotely so much more now. I decided to paint the walls this really deep, moody green. It's called "Billiard Green," I think? But honestly, picking the paint was a nightmare. I went to Home Depot and stared at those little paper swatches for probably two hours. The guy working in the paint department definitely thought I was crazy. He kept coming over and asking if I needed help, and I was like, "No, I just need to figure out the exact undertone of this green!" Because if you get a green with too much yellow in it, it just looks like split pea soup when the afternoon light hits it. My neighbor painted her front door this horrible yellow-green color last spring, and every time I walk my dog past her house, I just cringe. I don't know how she lives with it. She also has these massive garden gnomes all over her front lawn, which is a whole other aesthetic choice I just cannot get behind.

But, um... sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, the checking. Yeah, so I just do that whole routine—re-opening, checking layers, re-saving, the mental walkthrough. It doesn't take up my entire day, but it definitely makes me so much slower, and like I said, I just feel a lot less free creatively. It's really just to stop that anxious feeling that I messed something up.

When you do your checking routine, do you feel that not doing it would lead to a mistake that you couldn't forgive yourself for, or that others would judge you harshly for, or is it mostly about calming that anxious feeling inside so you can move on with your day?

I feel like I'm repeating myself a little bit, but yeah, it really is mostly just to calm that anxious feeling so I can finally move on with my day. Before I submit any work now, I just have to do it—I’ll re-open the file, compare the layers, re-save it, and sometimes mentally walk through every design choice one more time. 

Which, actually, speaking of design choices, I was at Whole Foods yesterday and I saw this new brand of oat milk, and their typography was just... atrocious. They used Papyrus! Can you believe that? A national brand using Papyrus in this day and age. It’s like they just gave up. My typography professor in college, Professor Higgins, would have had an absolute meltdown if he saw it. He used to make us trace Helvetica letters by hand for hours just to understand the kerning. He was this tiny, terrifying man who always wore these oversized polka-dot bowties. I think he owned like fifty of them. One time he spilled a whole espresso on a student's final portfolio and didn't even apologize, he just told her the coffee stains gave it "character." 

But, um, anyway. Sorry, my mind just wanders. What I mean is, doing all that checking—the saving, the layers, the mental review—it doesn’t take over my whole day, but it does make me slower. And honestly, it just makes me feel a lot less free creatively.
